title: Work practice
hookLine: cleaning, gardening and cooking as meditation

cards: The tools have gone missing. That's how a story about the Chan teacher Baizhang begins, as tradition tells it. He's old, and his students worry about him working in the fields, so they hide his hoe and his rake.
Baizhang doesn't argue. He just doesn't eat that day. When they ask why, the answer that has come down is short: a day without work is a day without food.
The tools come back. In Zen monasteries today, a whole period is set aside for what Baizhang refused to give up. Today's word: samu.

teach.b: First, what samu is. It's the work period in a Zen monastery or retreat: sweeping, raking, scrubbing floors, weeding, chopping vegetables, cleaning toilets.
It's done in silence, usually for a set stretch of the day, and everyone takes part, teachers included.

teach.h: THE BROOM IS THE CUSHION NOW.
teach.b: Second, the broom is the cushion now. Chores aren't a break from meditation; meditation doesn't stop when you pick up a broom.
The attention that watched the breath now watches the bristles on the floor, the water in the bucket, the weed coming up with its roots.
Third, no nice jobs, no rushing. Nobody is meant to rush to finish, and nobody picks the nice job. You're handed a task and do it fully, whether it's polishing a statue or unclogging a drain.
Some teachers say the toilets are a good place to see your own mind: what you resist is right there in the bucket.

teach.h: THE DISHES MIGHT BE THE PRACTICE.
teach.b: Fourth, the dishes might be the practice.

Baizhang's line ties the meal to the work, and the work to the way. Feeding the community and keeping it clean is the practice, not a distraction from it. So a sink full of dishes isn't standing between you and practice.
It might be the practice, if you let it.

how: In Zen monasteries and at many retreats, a daily work period called samu has everyone, teachers included, clean, garden and cook in silence, treating the work as meditation rather than a break from it.

o: chores that monks do as a break from meditation
a punishment of hard labor for a careless monk
work done in silence and full attention, as practice

p: a day without work, a day without food
the old teacher skips his meal

s: samu is a break from meditation
it's meditation carried into work: the same attention, on the broom.

games.q: you're old and respected. your students, out of kindness, hide your garden tools so you'll rest. what do you do?
games.why: as tradition tells it, Baizhang skipped his meal: a day without work, a day without food. the tools came back.

practice: Clean one small thing within reach, slowly and with full attention: a phone screen, a cup, a corner of the table, your glasses.
Feel the cloth against the surface, notice the moment your mind wants to hurry or drift to the next thing, and come back to this one surface. When it's clean, set it down and sit with the breath.

wordCard.voice: Samu. Work practice in Zen: cleaning, gardening, cooking, done in silence and with full attention, as meditation in motion. Today's word.

orig.note: Japanese: samu, the work period in a Zen monastery.

carryVoice: Your line: work is zen. No work, no food, and no chore outside the way. See you tomorrow, broom and all.

sources.ref: Baizhang Huaihai: the hidden tools and 'a day without work, a day without food'
